  <h1>Inside a Small Regenerative Farm Doing Things Differently</h1>
  <div class="tour-categories">
    <span class="tour-category">Florida</span>

    <span class="tour-category">Farm Tours</span>

    Tour Green Flamingo Organics in Oak Hill, Florida, where Liz uses regenerative

    market, local stores, restaurants, and the surrounding community.
  </p>
  <div class="tour-meta">
    <div><span class="meta-label">Host</span><span class="meta-value">Liz at Green Flamingo Organics</span></div>

  </div>

<p class="tour-lead">
Green Flamingo Organics is a small regenerative farm in Oak Hill, Florida,
where Liz and her team grow diversified produce using practices designed to
build soil rather than repeatedly disturb it. Across about 2.75 acres, the farm
combines succession planting, companion planting, seed saving, cover crops,
tarping, compost, hand tools, CSA production, and community programs into a
system with lessons for both working farmers and backyard growers.
</p>

<section class="quick-facts" aria-label="Tour quick facts">
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Farm</span><span class="fact-value">Green Flamingo Organics</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Host</span><span class="fact-value">Liz</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Location</span><span class="fact-value">Oak Hill, Florida</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Growing Since</span><span class="fact-value">2009 on This Property</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Farm Size</span><span class="fact-value">About 2.75 Acres</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Farm Season</span><span class="fact-value">Typically November–May</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Growing Style</span><span class="fact-value">Regenerative & No-Till</span></div>
  <div class="fact-card"><span class="fact-label">Community</span><span class="fact-value">CSA, WWOOF & Giving Garden</span></div>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>Inside a Small Regenerative Florida Farm</h2>
<p>
Green Flamingo Organics has been growing on this Oak Hill property since 2009.
The farm sells organic produce through a CSA, farmers market, health food stores,
and local restaurants, but the most interesting part of the tour is how that
food is produced.
</p>
<p>
Liz describes the farm as regenerative and no-till. Instead of relying on
frequent soil disturbance, the farm uses cover crops, compost, tarps, hand
tools, crop diversity, and living roots to build fertility and prepare beds.
Even within individual production beds, multiple crops are often grown together.
</p>
<p>
The farm is also smaller than it may appear. Liz estimates the area they use
at about 2.75 acres, and at any given time roughly half of that ground is in
cover crop while the other half is used for production.
</p>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>What You’ll Learn From Green Flamingo Organics</h2>
<div class="learn-grid">
  <div class="learn-item">Why succession planting every few weeks can keep favorite crops producing throughout a season</div>
  <div class="learn-item">How companion planting and diversified beds can help reduce insect pressure</div>
  <div class="learn-item">Why Liz leaves roots and plant material in place to support soil life and beneficial insects</div>
  <div class="learn-item">How tarping can prepare beds without tilling while leaving organic material on the soil</div>
  <div class="learn-item">How long-term seed saving can help crops adapt to a farm’s climate, soil, and harvest style</div>
  <div class="learn-item">Why Green Flamingo keeps roughly half its growing area in diverse cover crops</div>
</div>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>Growing More Through Diversity and Succession Planting</h2>
<p>
One of the clearest ideas in the tour is that production does not have to mean
planting large blocks of a single crop. Liz shows beds containing carrots,
turnips, kale, flowering kale, lettuce, and other crops together. That diversity
is intentional: crops such as turnips can experience heavier insect pressure
when planted in large uninterrupted rows, while mixing crops can reduce that pressure.
</p>
<p>
The same thinking applies over time. Green Flamingo succession-plants crops
such as cilantro, radish, turnips, and carrots every three to four weeks instead
of planting the entire season’s supply at once. For a home gardener, the same
idea can extend harvests instead of having everything mature at once.
</p>
<p>
The farm also adjusts its crop mix based on years of experience. Liz explains
that some mustards once used heavily in salad mix did not hold up as well
through washing and bagging, so the farm shifted toward crops with stronger
texture and better post-harvest quality.
</p>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>Building Soil Without Tilling</h2>
<p>
Green Flamingo prepares production beds with tarps instead of tilling. Liz says
that in their Florida climate, roughly three weeks under a tarp is often enough
to eliminate most existing growth. When the tarp is removed, the dead plant
material remains on the soil surface rather than being mechanically mixed into
the ground.
</p>
<p>
Liz compares the process to lifting a log or rock in nature. The soil underneath
stays cooler and moister, decomposition happens more slowly, and life continues
beneath the covered surface. For transplants, a bed can often be planted directly
after tarping; for tiny direct-seeded crops, surface material can be moved aside.
</p>
<p>
Leaving roots in the ground follows the same philosophy. Finished crops may
remain temporarily as habitat for beneficial insects and as living or decomposing
root material rather than being immediately pulled out.
</p>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>Cover Crops, Seed Saving, and Farming for the Long Term</h2>
<p>
Green Flamingo devotes a large share of its limited acreage to soil-building.
Liz explains that roughly half the farm is in cover crop at any given time.
Some areas move through multiple rounds of summer and winter cover crops and
rest for well over a year before returning to production.
</p>
<p>
Those cover-crop mixes are intentionally diverse, often containing nine to
twelve species. Grasses such as wheat, barley, rye, and oats are combined with
legumes such as peas, clovers, and alfalfa, while turnips and daikon radishes
add roots and biomass. A flail mower eventually turns the standing cover crop
into a mulch layer on the surface.
</p>
<p>
Seed saving adds another long-term layer. Liz has saved seed from one flowering
kale variety for almost a decade and says it has become well adapted to the
farm’s climate, soils, and the way the crop is harvested.
</p>
</section>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>Crops and Growing Systems Featured at Green Flamingo Organics</h2>
<p>
The tour takes place during the transition from Florida’s cool-season crops
into warmer spring production. The beds, greenhouse spaces, and cover-crop
areas show crops being harvested alongside plants intentionally left to flower,
set seed, support insects, or contribute biomass.
</p>

<section class="tour-section">
<h2>The Green Yard Takeaway</h2>
<div class="takeaway">
<p>
What stands out at Green Flamingo Organics is that regenerative farming is not
presented as one special technique. It is a collection of choices: keeping
living roots in the ground, rotating production with cover crops, diversifying
beds, saving seed, preparing soil without tilling, and continually adjusting
what is grown based on what the farm learns.
</p>
<p>
Those ideas are useful beyond a commercial farm. A backyard grower can
succession-plant cilantro, mix crops instead of planting a single block, save
seed from plants that perform well, leave roots in the soil, or use a cover
crop during an off-season.
</p>
</div>
</section>
